subject: I can not draw random variables from 3 components mixture model well.

messages.author: c6ba05975822c456
messages.subject: I can not draw random variables from 3 components mixture model well.
parts:
Hi, Stan developers.

I'm trying to draw  random variables from 3 components mixture model:

theta ~ 1/4*N(10, 0.01) + 1/2*N(0, 0.01) + 1/4*N(0, 0.01).


To draw random variables from the distribution above, I wrote Stan code bellow:

parameters{
  real theta;
}
model{
  real pk[3];
  pk[1] = log(0.25) + normal_lpdf(theta | -10, 0.01);
  pk[2] = log(0.50) + normal_lpdf(theta | 0, 0.01);
  pk[3] = log(0.25) + normal_lpdf(theta | 10, 0.01);
  target += log_sum_exp(pk);
}

R code is written as

d.model_test <- stan_model("test.stan")
result_test <- sampling(d.model_test, data=d.dat, iter=10000, chains=4)


However, it seems that I can only draw from N(0, 0.01) as like attached Rplot.png.
Is there a mistake?

Best regards.

messages.author: 29ce8550baceaeb0
messages.subject: Re: I can not draw random variables from 3 components mixture model well.
parts:
Interesting. Stan doesn't "draw" random variables from distributions--the particle needs
to be able to transition from one part of the density to another. At a guess, the issue here 
is might be that there is so little probability mass between the mixtures that it has difficulty
making its way around. 

If you use a larger scale (say, 1 rather than .01) it should work. If what you are trying to do is
approximate a dirac delta function, then you'll have a bit of trouble. This thread might help
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/rachael$20dirac%7Csort:relevance/stan-users/BkVJanzue4U/eN4CmGHtAAAJ

Jim

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: I can not draw random variables from 3 components mixture model well.
parts:
Hi Tomoki,

I'll answer your email directly -- I'm not going to try to read into what you're actually trying to accomplish.

To do what you want, this is what test.stan could look like:
transformed data {
  simplex[3] p;
  p[1] = 0.25;
  p[2] = 0.5;
  p[3] = 0.25;
}
model {
}
generated quantities {
  real theta;
  {
    int mixture_component;
    mixture_component = categorical_rng(p);
    if (mixture_component == 1)
      theta = normal_rng(-10, 0.01);
    else if (mixture_component == 2)
      theta = normal_rng(0, 0.01);
    else
      theta = normal_rng(10, 0.01);
  }
}

And the R code that goes along with it:
library(rstan)
fit <- stan("test.stan", algorithm="Fixed_param")
stan_hist(fit, "theta")

Notice, there are no parameters in the model that I've generated. That's why I've used the "Fixed_param" algorithm. Everything is in the generated quantities block. In fact, if you wanted to do probabilistic programming or just write a data generating process, it can all sit inside the generated quantities block. There's no need for it to go into the model.


Daniel

parts: Hi Tomoki,

On Nov 30, 2016, at 1:19 AM, Tomoki <t.matsu...@gmail.com> wrote:

Thank you for answering my question.

The existence of "Fixed_param" is new to me.
It's not emphasized much. It was put together for generating data.

In really, I would like to get samples from such as the following distribution:

p(\theta) \propto \prod_{i=1}^{10} ( 1/4 N(\theta|\mu_{1i}, 0.01) + 1/2 N(\mu_{2i}, 0.01) + 1/4 N(\mu_{3i}, 0.01) ) .

Thanks for writing out the math, but you're missing a lot of terms. It would help a lot if you generated simulated data, indicated which are parameters you want to infer and which are data.

In the math, the left hand side isn't just p(theta). It should be p(theta, mu_11, mu_21, ...), but more importantly, theta doesn't appear on the right hand side. If that's the case, then it looks like you know each of the mus and this can be written using generated quantities really easily.


But I'm not sure that's your intent. What would really help is to generate fake data with a script and mark which things are known and unknown. This is equivalent to creating a data generating process and labeling which are data and parameters.
In this case, how I write Stan code?
If you're just trying to simulate, then you could do this easily with two categorical_rng() calls in the generated quantities block.

Best regards.

If that's really what you're trying to do, this is easy. First, you really don't need to use Stan for this and Stan isn't really designed for this, but you can still do it. See below.
Even in this case, can I simulate \theta from the distribution above by coding in the generated quantities block?

Yes.

Set up data in R:
library(rstan)
stan_data <- list(mu = array(1:30, c(10, 3)))
fit <- stan("test.stan", data = stan_data, algorithm="Fixed_param")


test.stan:
data {
  vector[3] mu[10];

}
transformed data {
  simplex[3] p;
  p[1] = 0.25;
  p[2] = 0.5;
  p[3] = 0.25;
}
model {
}
generated quantities {
  real theta;

int index;
  int mixture_component;

  index = categorical_rng(rep_vector(0.1, 10));
  mixture_component = categorical_rng(p);
  theta = normal_rng(mu[index, mixture_component], 0.01);
}


Does that make sense?

p(\theta) \propto \prod_{i=1}^{10} ( 1/4 N(\theta|\mu_{1i}, 0.01) + 1/2 N(\mu_{2i}, 0.01) + 1/4 N(\mu_{3i}, 0.01) ) .

Thanks for writing out the math, but you're missing a lot of terms. It would help a lot if you generated simulated data, indicated which are parameters you want to infer and which are data.

In the math, the left hand side isn't just p(theta). It should be p(theta, mu_11, mu_21, ...), but more importantly, theta doesn't appear on the right hand side. If that's the case, then it looks like you know each of the mus and this can be written using generated quantities really easily.


But I'm not sure that's your intent. What would really help is to generate fake data with a script and mark which things are known and unknown. This is equivalent to creating a data generating process and labeling which are data and parameters. 


In this case, how I write Stan code?


If you're just trying to simulate, then you could do this easily with two categorical_rng() calls in the generated quantities block. 

Best regards.


2016年11月30日水曜日 13時59分21秒 UTC+9 Daniel Lee:
Hi Tomoki,

I'll answer your email directly -- I'm not going to try to read into what you're actually trying to accomplish.

To do what you want, this is what test.stan could look like:
transformed data {
  simplex[3] p;
  p[1] = 0.25;
  p[2] = 0.5;
  p[3] = 0.25;
}
model {
}
generated quantities {
  real theta;
  {
    int mixture_component;
    mixture_component = categorical_rng(p);
    if (mixture_component == 1)
      theta = normal_rng(-10, 0.01);
    else if (mixture_component == 2)
      theta = normal_rng(0, 0.01);
    else
      theta = normal_rng(10, 0.01);
  }
}

And the R code that goes along with it:
library(rstan)
fit <- stan("test.stan", algorithm="Fixed_param")
stan_hist(fit, "theta")

Notice, there are no parameters in the model that I've generated. That's why I've used the "Fixed_param" algorithm. Everything is in the generated quantities block. In fact, if you wanted to do probabilistic programming or just write a data generating process, it can all sit inside the generated quantities block. There's no need for it to go into the model.


Daniel

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] I can not draw random variables from 3 components mixture model well.
parts:
If you need to do inference on a three-component mixture like this
to infer values for the mu parameters or theta, then you want to
do this:

for (n in 1:10) {
real lps[3];
lps[1] = log(0.25) + normal_lpdf(theta | mu1[i], 0.01);
lps[2] = log(0.5) + ...
lps[3] = log(0.25) + ...
target += log_sum_exp(lps);
}

where that real lps declaration needs to be at the top of a block.

We're close to being able to add array expression to Stan, which will allow
the above to be rewritten as:

for (n in 1:10)
target += log_sum_exp({ log(0.25) + normal_lpdf(theta | mu1[i], 0.01),
...,
log(0.25) + ... });

- Bob
